body.hook: Stand in a long hallway and look down it. The walls, floor and ceiling lines all seem to rush toward one point in the distance. Renaissance artists figured out the rules for this around 600 years ago, and it changed art forever.

study.title: Into the Distance
study.question: How does one-point perspective create depth?
study.passage:
Studio steps (written for this lesson):
1. Look: Study Leonardo da Vinci's The Last Supper (about 1495–1498); all the lines of the room lead to a point near Jesus's head. Discuss how this guides the eye.
2. Boxes (15 minutes): Draw a horizon line across the page and a vanishing point (VP) in the middle. Draw five rectangles: above, below and on the horizon line. From each corner, draw light orthogonal lines to the VP. Add a back edge parallel to the front to finish each 3-D box. Erase the extra lines.
3. Room or hallway (30 minutes): Draw a back wall rectangle around the VP. Connect its corners to the corners of the page. Add doors, windows, floor tiles and a table, making every depth line go to the VP and keeping verticals vertical and horizontals horizontal.
Tip: use a ruler and draw guide lines lightly.
study.source: Original activity written for this lesson; teachers show an image of The Last Supper from a public museum source.

body.objective: Students will be able to draw in two-point perspective.

successCriteria: I can draw forms in two-point perspective

body.hook: Stand at a street corner and look at a building. You don't see its face straight on; you see two sides going away in two directions. That needs two vanishing points, and it's how architects and game designers draw corners.

vocabulary.definition: Perspective with two vanishing points, used when looking at a corner.
The vertical edge closest to the viewer, drawn first.

To come together at a point.

study.title: Corner View
study.question: How does two-point perspective show objects from an angle?
study.passage:
Studio steps (written for this lesson):
1. Setup: Draw a horizon line. Place VP1 near the left edge and VP2 near the right edge. Keep them far apart to avoid distortion.
2. Box (10 minutes): Draw a vertical line (the leading edge) between the VPs. Connect its top and bottom to both VPs. Draw two more verticals to mark the box's sides. Connect their tops to the opposite VPs to make the top surface.
3. Viewpoints (10 minutes): Draw the same box three times: horizon high (bird's-eye view), middle, and low (worm's-eye view).
4. Building corner (30 minutes): Draw a building from the corner: walls going to VP1 and VP2, windows and doors following the same lines, a sidewalk and a second smaller building behind. Keep all verticals vertical.

body.objective: Students will be able to add detail and value to a perspective drawing.
body.iCan: I can add detail and value to a perspective drawing.
successCriteria: I can add consistent light and shadow to a perspective drawing
I can add texture and detail that follow perspective

body.hook: A perspective drawing with only lines looks like a diagram. Add shadows, textures and details and it becomes a place you could walk into. Today you turn your perspective drawing into a finished artwork.

vocabulary.definition: Where the light comes from in a drawing.
Shading all surfaces as if lit by the same light source.
Placing one object in front of another to show depth.

study.title: Bring It to Life
study.question: How do value and detail turn a perspective drawing into a place?
study.passage:
Studio steps (written for this lesson):
1. Choose your light source and mark it with an arrow in the corner. Every surface facing it is light, surfaces facing away are mid-tone, and surfaces facing opposite are dark.
2. Shade surfaces (15 minutes): Use three values on every box or building: light, middle and dark, according to your light source.
3. Cast shadows (10 minutes): Add shadows on the ground falling away from the light.
4. Texture in perspective (15 minutes): Add bricks, wood grain, tiles or windows. Their lines must follow the perspective lines and get smaller and closer together as they go back.
5. Depth details (10 minutes): Add objects in the foreground (larger, detailed), middle ground and background (smaller, lighter, less detailed). Overlap at least two objects.
Example to study: M. C. Escher's prints, such as Relativity (1953), use perfect perspective and strong value contrast.
